\chapter{Head and Hand}
\label{ch:la-head-and-hand}
\hlchaptermodality{8}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say head and hand in Latin, and explain why manus is feminine when its declension usually is not.}

Say caput and manus with the correct gender, then list the manus words English still runs on.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[caput]{caput — the head, still working two thousand years later}

\label{lesson:LA-C08-caput}



\begin{quote}
Few Latin words stayed as busy in English as this one. And yet — one of Latin's own descendants \textbf{abandoned} it for the actual body part.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{caput, capitis} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{head}.\textquotedblright{} A perfectly ordinary noun, and one of Latin's most productive exports:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{English} & \textbf{literally} \\
\midrule
\textbf{cap}tain & the \textquotedblleft{}head\textquotedblright{} of a ship or unit \\
\textbf{cap}ital & the \textquotedblleft{}head\textquotedblright{} city, or the \textquotedblleft{}head\textquotedblright{} sum of money \\
de\textbf{cap}itate & to remove the head \\
\textbf{cap}itulate & to arrange terms under \textquotedblleft{}little-head\textquotedblright{} headings — hence, to yield \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Spanish kept \emph{caput} as its everyday word too: \textbf{cabeza} descends from it (by way of Vulgar Latin \emph{capitia}).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
French had \emph{caput} available — and \textbf{dropped it} for the body part entirely. Instead French says \textbf{tête}, from Latin \textbf{testa}, \textquotedblleft{}an earthenware pot, a shell.\textquotedblright{} Roman soldiers joked about the skull the way English speakers say \textquotedblleft{}noggin\textquotedblright{} (a small mug), and in Gaul, that joke eventually \textbf{replaced} \emph{caput} as the everyday word. \emph{Caput} didn't disappear from French, though — it survives there too, just not for the actual head: \textbf{chef} (\textquotedblleft{}chief\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{chapitre}, \textbf{capital}, \textbf{capitaine}.

So three languages took three different paths with the very same word: \textbf{Spanish} kept \emph{caput} as the plain, everyday \textquotedblleft{}head\textquotedblright{}; \textbf{French} demoted it to \textquotedblleft{}chief/chapter/capital\textquotedblright{} and reached for a pot-joke instead; \textbf{English} never used it for the body part at all, only for these borrowed \textquotedblleft{}head of something\textquotedblright{} senses.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}caput, capitis\textquotedblright{} — head
  \item the English family — \textquotedblleft{}captain, capital, decapitate, capitulate\textquotedblright{}
  \item the twist — French swapped \emph{caput} out for \emph{testa}, \textquotedblleft{}pot\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{caput} mean, and what English words come from it? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Head\textquotedblright{}} — \emph{captain, capital, decapitate, capitulate}.) Did every Romance language keep it as the everyday word for \textquotedblleft{}head\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{No} — Spanish did (\emph{cabeza}); French replaced it with \textbf{testa}, \textquotedblleft{}pot,\textquotedblright{} soldiers' slang for the skull.) Where does \emph{caput} survive in French, if not as \textquotedblleft{}head\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Chef, chapitre, capital, capitaine}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[manus]{manus — the hand, and a famous grammatical exception}

\label{lesson:LA-C08-manus}



\begin{quote}
Here's a word that's productive in English \emph{and} grammatically odd in Latin itself — an oddity that then rode straight through into Spanish.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{manus, manūs} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{hand}.\textquotedblright{} It belongs to Latin's \textbf{4th declension} — a group of nouns ending in \emph{-us} that runs \textbf{overwhelmingly masculine}: \emph{frūctus} (\textquotedblleft{}fruit\textquotedblright{}), \emph{exercitus} (\textquotedblleft{}army\textquotedblright{}), \emph{senātus} (\textquotedblleft{}senate\textquotedblright{}), \emph{portus} (\textquotedblleft{}port\textquotedblright{}) are all masculine. \textbf{Manus is one of only a handful of exceptions} in that declension — feminine, alongside \emph{anus} (\textquotedblleft{}old woman\textquotedblright{}) and \emph{domus} (\textquotedblleft{}house,\textquotedblright{} though \emph{domus} is even messier: it mixes 4th- and 2nd-declension endings throughout its own paradigm) — for reasons tied to each noun's own ancient history, not a rule you could predict from the \emph{-us} ending alone.

That oddity didn't stay buried in Latin grammar books: Spanish's word for hand, \textbf{mano}, inherited \emph{manus}'s feminine gender directly — which is exactly why \emph{mano} is famously feminine despite ending in \textbf{-o}, the ending that signals \emph{masculine} in nearly every other Spanish noun. One small Latin exception, carried whole into a completely different pattern in a daughter language, centuries later.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{cousinweb}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{English} & \textbf{literally} \\
\midrule
\textbf{manual} & done by hand \\
\textbf{manufacture} & made by hand (\emph{manus} + \emph{facere}, \textquotedblleft{}to make\textquotedblright{}) \\
\textbf{manuscript} & written by hand (\emph{manus} + \emph{scrībere}) \\
\textbf{maintain} & hold in the hand (\emph{manū tenēre}) \\
\textbf{manage} & to handle \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}manus, manūs\textquotedblright{} — hand
  \item the exception — \textquotedblleft{}feminine, unlike frūctus, exercitus, senātus\textquotedblright{}
  \item the English family — \textquotedblleft{}manual, manufacture, maintain, manage\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What gender is \textbf{manus}, and is that typical for its declension? (\textbf{Feminine} — unusual, since the 4th declension runs mostly \textbf{masculine}; \emph{manus} is one of a few exceptions, alongside \emph{domus} and \emph{anus}.) What Spanish word inherited this exact oddity? (\textbf{Mano} — feminine despite ending in \emph{-o}.) Give an English word from \emph{manus}. (\textbf{Manual, manufacture, manuscript, maintain, manage}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
